content: 1. Data from 234 participants in one randomized controlled trial (RCT) suggests that mass drug administration (MDA) likely reduces the prevalence of Plasmodium vivax parasites within one month post-MDA. The absolute difference was 49 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals, with a confidence interval (CI) of 95% ranging from 250 fewer to 163 fewer cases. However, the certainty of this evidence is moderate due to a serious risk of bias. 2. Data from 5,102 participants across six RCTs indicates that MDA may reduce the prevalence of Plasmodium falciparum parasites in low to very low transmission areas 4–12 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 16 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 8 fewer to 4 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is low due to serious risks of bias and inconsistency. 3. Data from 2,672 participants in five RCTs suggests that MDA may reduce the prevalence of Plasmodium vivax parasites 1–3 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 113 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 119 fewer to 101 fewer cases. The certainty of this evidence is low due to serious risks of bias and inconsistency. 4. Data from 6,255 participants in five RCTs suggests that MDA may have little to no effect on the prevalence of Plasmodium vivax parasites 4–12 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 1 more case per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 12 fewer to 17 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is low due to serious risks of bias and inconsistency. 5. Data from 243 participants in one RCT suggests that MDA may have little to no effect on the prevalence of Plasmodium vivax parasites 12–24 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 33 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 98 fewer to 84 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is low due to serious risks of bias and imprecision. 6. Data from 449 participants in one observational (non-randomized) study suggests that we are uncertain whether MDA increases or decreases the prevalence of Plasmodium vivax parasites within one month post-MDA. The absolute difference was 48 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 62 fewer to 9 fewer cases. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to a serious risk of bias. 7. Data from 1,024 participants in two observational studies suggests that we are uncertain whether MDA increases or decreases the prevalence of Plasmodium vivax parasites 1–3 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 189 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 208 fewer to 155 fewer cases. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to a very serious risk of bias. 8. Data from 939 participants in one observational study suggests that we are uncertain whether MDA increases or decreases the prevalence of Plasmodium vivax parasites 4–12 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 47 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to a very serious risk of bias. 9. Data from 6,911 participants in one RCT suggests that MDA probably increases the risk of serious adverse events (SAEs) within 0–3 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 308 more cases per 1 million individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 173 fewer to 564 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. 10. Data from 6,911 participants in one RCT suggests that MDA probably increases the risk of SAEs 4–12 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 1,528 fewer cases per 1 million individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 25,065 fewer to 2,180 fewer cases. The certainty of this evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. 11. Data from 90 participants in one RCT suggests that we are uncertain whether MDA increases or decreases adverse events 1–3 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 200 more cases per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 39 fewer to 571 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is very low. 12. Data from 703 participants in one RCT suggests that MDA with SP+AS, with or without PQ, probably increases vomiting. The absolute difference was 19 fewer cases per 1,000 individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 35 fewer to 22 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is moderate due to serious imprecision. 13. Data from 680 participants in one RCT suggests that MDA improves the difference in hemoglobin levels between day 1 and day 7 post-MDA treatment. The certainty of this evidence is high, with no serious inconsistency, indirectness, or publication bias, but very serious imprecision due to wide confidence intervals. 14. Data from five RCTs indicates that adverse events in low/very low transmission settings were inconsistently reported. For example, Morris (2018) reported no SAEs, while Shekalaghe (2011) reported two SAEs (a serious skin reaction and severe anemia). Eisele (2020) reported four SAEs, three of which were unrelated to drug ingestion. McLean (2021) reported six SAEs, including three deaths unrelated to the drug, one stillbirth, one miscarriage, and one episode of severe dehydration secondary to vomiting and diarrhea. 15. Von Seidlein (2019) reported that 19% of MDA participants recalled adverse events, with 35% of these considered related to antimalarials. The most common complaints were dizziness (23%), nausea (8%), vomiting (4%), and itching (2%). 16. Eisele (2020) reported 687 adverse events among 336,821 courses of DHA-P, while McLean (2021) reported 151 adverse events out of 10,677 doses, most of which were mild (e.g., dizziness and rash). Only 18 events were deemed probably related to the medicine. 17. Data from one RCT suggests that drug resistance, specifically PfKelch13 mutations, was rare among those who received MDA. At baseline, 269 patients with Plasmodium falciparum were identified, and one month post-MDA, only one infection (7%) showed the PfKelch13 genotype. The certainty of this evidence is low due to very serious imprecision. 18. Data from 7,541,000 participants in one observational study suggests that we are uncertain about the effect of MDA on all-cause mortality across all ages within one month post-MDA. The absolute difference was 26 fewer cases per 1 million individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 35 fewer to 15 fewer cases. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias. 19. Data from 1,353,070 participants in one observational study suggests that we are uncertain about the effect of MDA on all-cause mortality in children under five years of age within one month post-MDA. The absolute difference was 165 fewer cases per 1 million individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 187 fewer to 132 fewer cases. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias. 20. Data from 11,419,200 participants in one observational study suggests that we are uncertain about the effect of MDA on all-cause mortality across all ages 1–3 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 36 more cases per 1 million individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 25 more to 48 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 21. Data from 2,008,720 participants in one observational study suggests that we are uncertain about the effect of MDA on all-cause mortality in children under five years of age 1–3 months post-MDA. The absolute difference was 12 more cases per 1 million individuals, with a CI of 95% ranging from 12 fewer to 42 more cases. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias and imprecision. 22. Data from one observational study suggests that all-cause hospital admissions decreased by 5–21% during the four weeks after the first round of MDA and by 8–19% during the four weeks after the second round of MDA. However, statistically significant changes were observed at only one of eight time points. Absolute effects could not be calculated due to a lack of data on sample sizes and non-MDA control areas. The certainty of this evidence is very low due to serious risk of bias.
